How Much Sleep Do Founders Actually Need?
The claim that founders need only four hours, what the research says, and the minimum amount that research supports.
How Much Sleep Do Founders Actually Need?

For a long time, sleeping as little as possible was treated as a sign of commitment in startup culture. Founders told stories of four hour nights. That view is changing because of sleep research. If you have asked how much sleep founders need, the research based answer is more than most founders get, and far more than four hours.
The claim that founders need only four hours of sleep
The idea that high performers need less sleep is persistent, and it rests on two misunderstandings.

The first is that some people genuinely need little sleep. A small number do. Researchers led by Ying Hui Fu at UC San Francisco have identified rare genetic variants that allow carriers to feel well and perform well on around six hours. Rare is the important word. These variants are found in a tiny fraction of the population. The chance that you, or the founder whose routine you read about, carry one is very low.

The second misunderstanding is that feeling fine means performing well. In controlled studies, people restricted to short sleep for weeks report only slight sleepiness while their measured performance keeps falling. People who sleep little are often not adapted. They have lost the ability to notice how impaired they are.
In laboratory studies, people restricted to six hours a night felt only slightly sleepy while their measured performance fell steadily for two weeks.
What the research of Matthew Walker says
Matthew Walker, professor of neuroscience and psychology at UC Berkeley and author of
Why We Sleep

, did more than anyone to bring sleep science into business discussions. His central argument is that sleep is not a passive state of rest. It is an active period of biological work that cannot be skipped without cost.

Some of the more dramatic claims in his book have been challenged by other researchers, and it is worth reading it with that in mind. The core of his argument reflects a broad scientific consensus. Work from his laboratory showed that a single night of sleep deprivation made the emotional centre of the brain far more reactive and weakened its link to the prefrontal cortex, which is used for rational thought. His wider message is direct. The number of people who can function on six hours of sleep or less without any impairment, rounded to a whole number, is effectively zero.

The major professional bodies agree. In 2015 the American Academy of Sleep Medicine and the Sleep Research Society published a joint consensus that adults should sleep seven or more hours a night on a regular basis for optimal health.
The joint consensus of the American Academy of Sleep Medicine and the Sleep Research Society: adults need seven or more hours of sleep a night, regularly.
Sleep stages, why founders need all stages
Sleep is not uniform. Across the night you cycle through stages roughly every 90 minutes, and each stage does different work. Founders rely on all of it.
Deep sleep and memory consolidation

Slow wave sleep, the deepest stage, is most common in the first half of the night. During it the brain replays and stabilises what you learned during the day, moving information from short term storage into long term memory. Details from a customer call, the structure of a financial model, and a new process you are learning are examples. Deep sleep helps make them stay in memory. It is also when the body does much of its physical repair.
REM sleep and emotional processing

REM sleep, concentrated in the last third of the night, is when most vivid dreaming happens. Walker has described REM sleep as helping the brain reprocess emotional experiences in a chemical environment low in stress chemicals, which reduces the emotional strength of difficult memories. A founder who regularly cuts sleep short loses a larger share of REM sleep, because REM comes at the end of the night. The result is often quicker irritation and emotions carrying over from one hard day to the next.
REM sleep and solving problems in new ways

REM sleep is also when unexpected connections form. In a study published in Nature, participants who slept between attempts at a problem were more than twice as likely to discover a hidden shortcut as those who stayed awake for the same length of time. Further work has linked REM sleep specifically to the ability to connect unrelated ideas. Work that requires finding an approach others have not seen needs the last two hours of the night.
People who slept on a problem were more than twice as likely to discover a hidden solution as those who stayed awake for the same period.
How much sleep do founders need, the minimum amount supported by research
In practice, use the consensus rather than the rare exceptions.
Seven hours asleep, not seven hours in bed

Most people take 15 to 20 minutes to fall asleep and wake briefly during the night. To get seven hours of actual sleep you typically need around seven and a half to eight hours in bed. Plan the window, not just the hours.
Consistency matters more than sleeping longer on weekends

Sleeping five hours during the week and ten hours at the weekend does not average out. Irregular sleep disrupts your circadian rhythm and leaves you feeling as if you have jet lag without travelling. Keep your wake time within an hour every day.
Protect the beginning and the end of the night
Late nights cut into REM. Very early alarms cut into REM too. If something has to give during a demanding week, borrow from the middle of the evening, not the end of the night.
Treat six hours as a warning sign

One short night is recoverable. A run of nights at six hours or less is when deficits in focus, mood and judgement start to accumulate. If you are there more than two nights a week, look at the cause. Our guide to
why founders can't sleep
covers the most common culprits.
Sleep is part of the work

Founders who continue working for a long time are not the ones who need the least sleep. They treat sleep as part of the work, because learning is stored, emotions are reset and new ideas form during sleep. That matters most when the stakes are highest, as we explore in
